title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
How long were patients followed?
Every survival paper reports the median follow-up. The obvious way to calculate it is wrong:

RPython



median(cohort$followup_years)        # misleading: revisions and deaths cut follow-up short

[1] 4.365

# reverse Kaplan-Meier: treat "still followed at the end" as the event
reverse_km <- survfit(Surv(followup_years, event_status == 0) ~ 1, data = cohort)
quantile(reverse_km, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), conf.int = FALSE)

  25   50   75 
3.52 5.62 7.93 





from lifelines.utils import qth_survival_times

print(cohort["followup_years"].median())   # misleading: revisions and deaths cut follow-up short

4.365

# reverse Kaplan-Meier: treat "still followed at the end" as the event
reverse_km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(cohort["followup_years"],
                                     event_observed=(cohort["event_status"] == 0))
print(qth_survival_times([0.75, 0.5, 0.25], reverse_km.survival_function_))   # 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles

      KM_estimate
0.75         3.52
0.50         5.62
0.25         7.93





The plain median, 4.4 years, mixes two things: how long the study watched patients, and how soon they were revised or died. A patient revised at 1 year wasn’t “followed for 1 year” in the sense readers care about. The study would have kept watching them.
The reverse Kaplan-Meier method answers the real question: how long would patients have been followed if nothing had happened to them? It swaps the roles: being censored at the end of follow-up becomes the “event”, and revisions and deaths become the censored observations. The median follow-up is 5.62 years (IQR 3.52 to 7.93).

Methods: Median follow-up was estimated with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method.
Results: The median follow-up was 5.62 years (IQR 3.52 to 7.93).

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
Comparing groups: the log-rank test
The log-rank test asks whether two or more survival curves differ. At every revision time it compares each group’s observed revisions with the number expected if all groups had the same risk, then adds up the differences across the whole follow-up. It’s the same test as the Mantel-Haenszel (or Mantel-Cox) test in the decision table.
Two groups. In total hips, does the surgical approach (anterior or posterior) affect revision?

RPython



tha <- cohort |> filter(procedure == "THA")        # approach applies to hips only

survfit2(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, data = tha, conf.type = "log-log") |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")







approach_logrank <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, data = tha)
approach_logrank

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, 
    data = tha)

                     N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
approach=anterior  145       18     20.9     0.397     0.912
approach=posterior 125       19     16.1     0.513     0.912

 Chisq= 0.9  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.3 





from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test

tha = cohort[cohort["procedure"] == "THA"]                # approach applies to hips only
anterior = tha[tha["approach"] == "anterior"]
posterior = tha[tha["approach"] == "posterior"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
km_anterior = KaplanMeierFitter(label="anterior").fit(anterior["followup_years"], anterior["revised"])
km_posterior = KaplanMeierFitter(label="posterior").fit(posterior["followup_years"], posterior["revised"])
km_anterior.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
km_posterior.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Revision-free survival")
add_at_risk_counts(km_anterior, km_posterior, ax=ax, rows_to_show=["At risk", "Events"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







approach_logrank = logrank_test(anterior["followup_years"], posterior["followup_years"],
                                event_observed_A=anterior["revised"], event_observed_B=posterior["revised"])
print(approach_logrank.test_statistic, approach_logrank.p_value)

0.9116386659614966 0.33968000597546394






Observed / Expected: the posterior hips had 19 revisions where 16.1 were expected; the anterior hips had 18 where 20.9 were expected.
Chisq = 0.9 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.340: no clear evidence that the curves differ over the whole follow-up.

But look at the plot. The posterior curve drops sharply in the first months, then the two curves come together (late on they even cross, where the CIs overlap widely). The early revisions are real: by 6 months, survivorship was 88.7% after the posterior approach and 98.6% after the anterior approach.

posterior 0.887 [0.817, 0.932]





The log-rank test adds up the differences over the whole follow-up. A large difference in the first months gets diluted by the years after, when the groups differ little, and the test can miss a real difference. Page 14 shows how to detect this and how to model it.
Three or more groups. The same test compares any number of groups. Does revision differ between implants A, B and C?

RPython



implant_logrank <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)
implant_logrank

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)

            N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
implant=A 246       25     34.0      2.40      4.15
implant=B 217       18     30.0      4.81      7.65
implant=C 137       38     16.9     26.17     33.18

 Chisq= 33.5  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 5e-08 





from lifelines.statistics import multivariate_logrank_test

implant_logrank = multivariate_logrank_test(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["implant"], cohort["revised"])
print(implant_logrank.test_statistic, implant_logrank.degrees_of_freedom, implant_logrank.p_value)

33.46861907356945 2 5.399850171504637e-08






Observed / Expected: implant C had 38 revisions where 16.9 were expected. Implants A (25 vs 34.0) and B (18 vs 30.0) had fewer than expected.
Chisq = 33.5 on 2 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001: at least one implant’s curve differs from the others. The test doesn’t say which; page 15 covers comparing pairs of groups. Page 8 gives each implant’s hazard ratio.


Methods: Revision-free survival was compared between groups with the log-rank test.
Results: The log-rank test for revision-free survival across implants gave χ² = 33.5 (df = 2, p < 0.001). In total hip arthroplasty, survivorship at 6 months was 88.7% (95% CI 81.7% to 93.2%) after the posterior approach and 98.6% (95% CI 94.5% to 99.6%) after the anterior approach (log-rank test over the whole follow-up, χ² = 0.9, df = 1, p = 0.340).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: always plot the curves before you trust the test



The log-rank test is most powerful when one group’s hazard is a steady multiple of the other’s over time (proportional hazards). When the curves cross, as with the surgical approach here, a non-significant test can hide a real difference. And don’t compare groups at one hand-picked time point to get a significant result: decide your time points before you look.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: one function or two



R’s survdiff() takes a formula and handles two groups or more. lifelines has logrank_test() for two groups, which takes each group’s data separately, and multivariate_logrank_test() for any number, which takes a grouping column. They give identical results.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
section: Competing risks: when patients die first
text:
Competing risks: when patients die first
So far, patients who died were treated as censored. That assumes they would have gone on to be revised at the same rate as everyone else. They can’t: a patient who has died can never be revised. Death is a competing risk.
With death treated as censored, 1 − Kaplan-Meier estimates the risk of revision in an imaginary world where nobody dies. In an older population, where many patients die during follow-up, it overstates the real proportion who will be revised. The cumulative incidence function (CIF), estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method, gives the real proportion: the chance of being revised by a given time, allowing for the chance of dying first.
The data need one status column with three values. In the cohort, event_status is 0 for censored, 1 for revised and 2 for died.

RPython



cohort <- cohort |>
  mutate(status = factor(event_status, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
                         labels = c("censored", "revision", "death")))   # censored must come first

# with a three-level status, survfit() estimates the cumulative incidences (Aalen-Johansen)
cif <- survfit2(Surv(followup_years, status) ~ 1, data = cohort, conf.type = "log-log")

cif |>
  ggcuminc(outcome = c("revision", "death")) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Cumulative incidence")







tidy_survfit(cif, times = c(2, 5, 10)) |>
  select(outcome, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  outcome   time estimate conf.low conf.high
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 death        2   0.0530   0.0369    0.0733
2 death        5   0.142    0.112     0.174 
3 death       10   0.240    0.193     0.290 
4 revision     2   0.0595   0.0423    0.0806
5 revision     5   0.128    0.100     0.159 
6 revision    10   0.193    0.153     0.237 

1 - summary(km, times = c(2, 5, 10))$surv    # 1 − Kaplan-Meier, for comparison

[1] 0.06071255 0.13690651 0.21968772





from scipy.stats import norm
from statsmodels.duration.survfunc import CumIncidenceRight

# event_status: 0 = censored, 1 = revision, 2 = death
cif = CumIncidenceRight(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["event_status"])
revision = pd.DataFrame({"cif": cif.cinc[0], "se": cif.cinc_se[0]}, index=cif.times)   # event type 1
death = pd.DataFrame({"cif": cif.cinc[1], "se": cif.cinc_se[1]}, index=cif.times)      # event type 2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.step(revision.index, revision["cif"], where="post", label="revision")
ax.step(death.index, death["cif"], where="post", label="death")
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative incidence")
legend = ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







z = norm.ppf(0.975)
for years in [2, 5, 10]:
    row = revision.loc[:years].iloc[-1]                                  # last step at or before that time
    spread = np.exp(z * row["se"] / (row["cif"] * np.log(row["cif"])))   # the log-log CI, as in R
    print(years, round(row["cif"], 3), round(row["cif"] ** (1 / spread), 3), round(row["cif"] ** spread, 3),
          round(1 - km.survival_function_at_times(years).iloc[0], 3))

2 0.059 0.042 0.081 0.061
5 0.128 0.1 0.159 0.137
10 0.193 0.153 0.237 0.22





Reading it: - The revision curve is the cumulative incidence of revision: 5.9% at 2 years, 12.8% at 5 years and 19.3% at 10 years. - The death curve rises faster: 24.0% of patients had died without a revision by 10 years. - 1 − Kaplan-Meier says 22.0% by 10 years. It overstates the real proportion revised by 2.7 percentage points, because it pretends the patients who died could still have been revised.
The gap grows with the number of deaths. It’s small at 2 years, when few patients have died, and largest in older patients (see exercise 2).
Comparing groups: Gray’s test (R only). Gray’s test is the competing-risks counterpart of the log-rank test: it compares cumulative incidence curves between groups. The tidycmprsk package runs it:

library(tidycmprsk)

cif_by_implant <- cuminc(Surv(followup_years, status) ~ implant, data = cohort)
glance(cif_by_implant) |>
  select(outcome_1, statistic_1, p.value_1, outcome_2, statistic_2, p.value_2)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  outcome_1 statistic_1   p.value_1 outcome_2 statistic_2 p.value_2
  <chr>           <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>
1 revision         31.5 0.000000142 death           0.969     0.616


The cumulative incidence of revision differed between implants (Gray’s test χ² = 31.5, df = 2, p < 0.001); there was no clear evidence that the cumulative incidence of death differed (χ² = 0.97, p = 0.616).

Methods: The cumulative incidence of revision was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method, treating death as a competing risk, and compared between implants with Gray’s test.
Results: The cumulative incidence of revision was 12.8% (95% CI 10.0% to 15.9%) at 5 years and 19.3% (95% CI 15.3% to 23.7%) at 10 years, when the cumulative incidence of death was 24.0% (95% CI 19.3% to 29.0%). Gray’s test for the cumulative incidence of revision across implants gave χ² = 31.5 (df = 2, p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: which number answers your question?



Both estimates are useful, but they answer different questions: - 1 − Kaplan-Meier answers “how well does the implant perform while patients are alive?” It’s the usual measure for comparing implants, and registries report it. - The cumulative incidence answers “what proportion of patients will actually be revised?” Use it to counsel patients or plan services, especially for older patients.
Say which one you report. Never call 1 − Kaplan-Meier “the proportion of patients revised” when many patients died.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: which tools




The cumulative incidence: R’s survfit() estimates it whenever the status has more than two levels. In Python, use statsmodels’ CumIncidenceRight(): it gives the estimates and their standard errors but no CI, so the code builds the same log-log CI as R. lifelines also has an AalenJohansenFitter, but it moves tied follow-up times by a small random amount, which can shift an estimate read at exactly 5 or 10 years, so we don’t use it.
Gray’s test: Python has no mature implementation of Gray’s test. Plot the curves in Python, but run the test in R. tidycmprsk’s cuminc() also gives the cumulative incidences, with a slightly different CI method.
Fine-Gray regression models the cumulative incidence with several predictors at once; it’s R only too (page 14).

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text: A test for three or more groups asks one question: “is there any difference among them?”. When the answer is yes, the next question is which groups differ from which. Answering it means running several tests at once, and every extra test is another chance of a false positive. This page shows how to compare groups in pairs while keeping that chance under control. Most “After …” sections pick up an example from page 8, page 9 or page 13.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text:
Why many tests mislead
A test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false positive when there is truly no difference. Run several tests and those chances accumulate. The chance of at least one false positive across a set of tests is the family-wise error rate. For independent tests at the 5% level it’s 1 − 0.95k, where k is the number of tests:

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tests <- c(1, 3, 6, 10, 20)
false_positives <- tibble(tests, chance_of_a_false_positive = round(1 - 0.95^tests, 2))
false_positives

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  tests chance_of_a_false_positive
  <dbl>                      <dbl>
1     1                       0.05
2     3                       0.14
3     6                       0.26
4    10                       0.4 
5    20                       0.64





import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import scikit_posthocs as sp
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.statistics import pairwise_logrank_test

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")

tests = np.array([1, 3, 6, 10, 20])
false_positives = pd.DataFrame({"tests": tests, "chance_of_a_false_positive": (1 - 0.95**tests).round(2)})

3     10                        0.40
4     20                        0.64





Four groups make six pairs. Six independent tests at the 5% level give a 26% chance of at least one false alarm, even when nothing is going on; twenty tests give 64%. Pairwise comparisons aren’t independent, because each group appears in three of the six pairs, so for four groups of equal size the chance is a little lower: about 20%. That’s still four times the 5% you meant to allow. Comparing pairs therefore needs an adjustment: a stricter rule that keeps the chance of any false positive across the whole set of comparisons at 5%.






Note💡 In plain language



Buy one lottery ticket and you’ll almost certainly lose. Buy twenty and your chance of winning something goes up. Each p-value below 0.05 is a small “win”, and with enough tests one will turn up by luck alone. Adjusting the p-values makes each win harder to get, so the overall chance stays where you set it.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: Adjusting p-values: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg
text:
Adjusting p-values: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg
Page 8 found that age differs across the four ASA classes. Here are the six pairwise comparisons, each a Welch t test, with the p-values left as they are (unadjusted) and then adjusted three ways:

RPython



age_pairs <- pairwise.t.test(cohort$age, cohort$asa, pool.sd = FALSE,      # Welch t tests
                             p.adjust.method = "none")
unadjusted <- age_pairs$p.value[lower.tri(age_pairs$p.value, diag = TRUE)]  # the six p-values, in pair order

adjusted <- tibble(pair = c("1 vs 2", "1 vs 3", "1 vs 4", "2 vs 3", "2 vs 4", "3 vs 4"),
                   unadjusted,
                   bonferroni = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "bonferroni"),
                   holm = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "holm"),
                   bh = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "BH"))
adjusted |> mutate(across(-pair, \(p) round(p, 4)))

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  pair   unadjusted bonferroni   holm     bh
  <chr>       <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 1 vs 2     0.022      0.132  0.0439 0.0263
2 1 vs 3     0          0      0      0     
3 1 vs 4     0          0      0      0     
4 2 vs 3     0          0      0      0     
5 2 vs 4     0.0002     0.0013 0.0007 0.0003
6 3 vs 4     0.0298     0.179  0.0439 0.0298





asa_pairs = list(itertools.combinations([1, 2, 3, 4], 2))
unadjusted = [stats.ttest_ind(cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == a, "age"], cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == b, "age"],
                              equal_var=False).pvalue                    # Welch t tests
              for a, b in asa_pairs]

adjusted = pd.DataFrame({
    "pair": [f"{a} vs {b}" for a, b in asa_pairs],
    "unadjusted": unadjusted,
    "bonferroni": multipletests(unadjusted, method="bonferroni")[1],
    "holm": multipletests(unadjusted, method="holm")[1],
    "bh": multipletests(unadjusted, method="fdr_bh")[1],
})
print(adjusted.round(4))

     pair  unadjusted  bonferroni    holm      bh
0  1 vs 2      0.0220      0.1317  0.0439  0.0263
1  1 vs 3      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
2  1 vs 4      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
3  2 vs 3      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
4  2 vs 4      0.0002      0.0013  0.0007  0.0003
5  3 vs 4      0.0298      0.1790  0.0439  0.0298





Follow the ASA 1 vs ASA 2 comparison across the row: - Unadjusted, p = 0.022: “significant” on its own, but it’s one of six tests. - Bonferroni, p = 0.132: multiplies every p-value by the number of tests (here 6). Simple, but the strictest: it often throws away real differences. - Holm, p = 0.044: a step-down version of Bonferroni. It multiplies the smallest p-value by 6, the next smallest by 5, and so on, but an adjusted p-value can’t be smaller than the one before it in that order. ASA 3 vs 4 has the largest unadjusted p-value (0.030), so it’s multiplied by 1, but it takes 0.044 from ASA 1 vs 2, the one before it. It controls the family-wise error rate just as well as Bonferroni and is never less powerful, so use Holm rather than Bonferroni. - Benjamini-Hochberg (BH), p = 0.026: controls something different, the false discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among the results you call significant. It’s the most lenient of the three. It suits screening many outcomes for leads, not confirming a claim.






Warning⚠️ Watch out: decide the adjustment before you see the p-values



Picking whichever adjustment keeps your favourite result significant is p-hacking. Choose in advance: Holm (or a method built for the test, like Tukey’s below) for comparisons you’ll report as findings, Benjamini-Hochberg only for exploratory screening. Say in the Methods which you used and how many comparisons it covered.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: After ANOVA: Tukey’s HSD and Games-Howell
text:
After ANOVA: Tukey’s HSD and Games-Howell
After a one-way ANOVA, Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) compares every pair of group means. It adjusts for all the pairs at once, and gives each difference a CI that’s adjusted too. It assumes the groups have similar spreads, like the ANOVA. When they don’t (the largest SD is more than about twice the smallest), use Games-Howell, the Welch version of Tukey’s test.

RPython



age_anova <- aov(age ~ factor(asa), data = cohort)
age_tukey <- TukeyHSD(age_anova)                          # diff, adjusted 95% CI, adjusted p
age_tukey

    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = age ~ factor(asa), data = cohort)

diff / meandiff: the difference in mean age between two ASA classes, in years.
lwr, upr / lower, upper: the 95% CI of that difference, adjusted for all six comparisons.
p adj / p-adj: the adjusted p-value.

Four of the six pairs differ clearly (p < 0.001 or, for ASA 2 vs 4 in the Games-Howell test, p = 0.001). Two don’t: ASA 2 patients were 3.6 years older than ASA 1 patients (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7, p = 0.096), and ASA 4 patients 5.3 years older than ASA 3 patients (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9, p = 0.072). Both CIs include 0, and both comparisons involve one of the two small classes. The SDs are similar (8.7 to 9.3 years), so Games-Howell reaches the same conclusions.

Methods: Age was compared across ASA classes with one-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s honestly significant difference test for pairwise comparisons.
Results: Across ASA classes, one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 596) = 23.9 (p < 0.001). In pairwise comparisons, the difference in mean age was 5.0 years between ASA 3 and ASA 2 (95% CI 3.0 to 6.9; p < 0.001), 3.6 years between ASA 2 and ASA 1 (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7; p = 0.096) and 5.3 years between ASA 4 and ASA 3 (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9; p = 0.072). Table 2 gives all six pairwise comparisons.







Tip🔀 R vs Python: Tukey and Games-Howell



R’s TukeyHSD() and statsmodels’ pairwise_tukeyhsd() give identical results; R writes the pairs as “2-1” (second group minus first), statsmodels as group1, group2 with meandiff = group2 − group1. For Games-Howell, R needs the rstatix package; in Python, pingouin’s pairwise_gameshowell() reports diff as A − B, so its signs are the reverse of R’s estimates. The p-values agree.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text:
After Kruskal-Wallis: Dunn’s test
Dunn’s test follows a Kruskal-Wallis test. It compares the groups’ mean ranks from the Kruskal-Wallis ranking, so it measures every pair on the same scale. Use it with Holm’s adjustment. Running separate Mann-Whitney tests instead re-ranks the data for each pair and needs an adjustment of its own.
Length of stay (LOS) is skewed (most patients go home on day 0 or 1), so it belongs in the rank column. Does it differ across ASA classes?

RPython



cohort |>
  group_by(asa) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(los_days),
            q1 = quantile(los_days, 0.25), q3 = quantile(los_days, 0.75))

los_kw

dunn = sp.posthoc_dunn(cohort, val_col="los_days", group_col="asa", p_adjust="holm")
print(dunn.round(4))                                           # adjusted p-values

        1       2       3       4

Kruskal-Wallis H = 24.3, df = 3, p < 0.001: LOS differs somewhere across the classes.
Dunn’s test: ASA 1 differs from every other class (adjusted p = 0.011 against ASA 2, p < 0.001 against ASAs 3 and 4), and ASA 2 differs from ASAs 3 (p = 0.047) and 4 (p = 0.022). There was no clear evidence of a difference between ASA 3 and 4 (p = 0.061).
The statistic in R’s output is a z score: positive means the second group’s ranks are higher (longer stays).


Results: The median length of stay was 0 days (IQR 0 to 0) in ASA 1 and 1 day (IQR 0.25 to 3.5) in ASA 4 (Kruskal-Wallis H = 24.3, df = 3, p < 0.001). In Dunn’s tests with Holm’s adjustment, p ≤ 0.011 for ASA 1 against each other class and p = 0.061 for ASA 3 against ASA 4.







Tip🔀 R vs Python: Dunn’s test



Both correct the z scores for tied ranks, which matter here because many patients share a LOS of 0 or 1 day, and both give the same adjusted p-values. R’s rstatix returns one row per pair; scikit-posthocs’ posthoc_dunn() returns a square table of p-values with the groups on both sides.

section: After chi-square: pairwise Fisher’s exact tests
text:
After chi-square: pairwise Fisher’s exact tests
After a chi-square (or Fisher) test on a table with three or more groups, compare the groups two at a time with Fisher’s exact test, then adjust with Holm. Take 90-day complications across the four ASA classes. Two of the expected counts are below 5, too few for the chi-square test (page 8), so the overall test is Fisher’s exact test too:

complications

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: After repeated-measures ANOVA: paired t tests
text:
After repeated-measures ANOVA: paired t tests
Page 9 found that PROMIS physical function changed over the first year, in 328 patients measured at all four visits. To say when it changed, compare every pair of visits with a paired t test and adjust with Holm:

RPython



pf <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, promis_pf) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(promis_pf))) |>                  # patients measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"))) |>
  arrange(case_id, visit)                           # paired tests match rows by position

pf_pairs <- rstatix::pairwise_t_test(pf, promis_pf ~ visit, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm")
pf_pairs |> select(group1, group2, n1, statistic, df, p.adj)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  group1 group2    n1 statistic    df    p.adj
  <chr>  <chr>  <int>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 preop  6wk      328     -7.98   327 4.87e-14
2 preop  3mo      328    -20.9    327 1.48e-61
3 preop  1yr      328    -28.7    327 1.58e-90
4 6wk    3mo      328    -12.8    327 2.45e-30
5 6wk    1yr      328    -20.7    327 5.15e-61
6 3mo    1yr      328     -7.51   327 5.59e-13





pf = proms[["case_id", "visit", "promis_pf"]]
pf = pf[pf.groupby("case_id")["promis_pf"].transform(lambda scores: scores.notna().all())]

pf_pairs = pg.pairwise_tests(data=pf, dv="promis_pf", within="visit", subject="case_id", padjust="holm")
print(pf_pairs[["A", "B", "T", "dof", "p_corr"]])

     A      B          T    dof        p_corr
0  1yr    3mo   7.512610  327.0  5.587418e-13
1  1yr    6wk  20.749915  327.0  5.152961e-61
2  1yr  preop  28.688297  327.0  1.577382e-90
3  3mo    6wk  12.834296  327.0  2.449999e-30
4  3mo  preop  20.914197  327.0  1.475132e-61
5  6wk  preop   7.983594  327.0  4.873879e-14





Every pair of visits differs (all adjusted p < 0.001): PROMIS physical function improved between each visit and the next, from pre-op to 6 weeks (t = 8.0) through to 3 months and 1 year (t = 7.5 for the last step). With 328 patients and changes this large, the adjustment changes nothing. It matters most when results sit near p = 0.05.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: which way round



pingouin sorts the visits alphabetically and subtracts the second from the first, so its t statistics are negative where R’s are positive, or the other way round. Compare their sizes. rstatix needs the rows in the same patient order within every visit, so sort by patient first.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: After Friedman: pairwise Wilcoxon or Conover tests
text:
After Friedman: pairwise Wilcoxon or Conover tests
After a Friedman test, compare pairs of visits with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Holm’s adjustment, or with Conover’s test, which reuses the Friedman ranks (as Dunn’s test does after Kruskal-Wallis) and is often more powerful. Page 9 found that the EFAS score changed between 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months in 50 patients with a boot:

RPython



efas_boot <- trial |>
  filter(arm == "boot", visit %in% c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo")) |>
  select(patient_id, visit, efas) |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(efas))) |>                         # patients scored at all three visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo"))) |>
  arrange(patient_id, visit)

efas_pairs <- rstatix::pairwise_wilcox_test(efas_boot, efas ~ visit, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE,
                                            p.adjust.method = "holm")
efas_pairs |> select(group1, group2, statistic, p, p.adj)

All three pairs differ (adjusted p < 0.001 with either method): the EFAS score rose between 6 weeks and 3 months and again between 3 months and 12 months.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: the statistic



R’s wilcox.test() reports V, the sum of the positive ranks; scipy reports the smaller of the two rank sums. Here both are the same number, because the later visit scores higher for most patients. Conover’s test needs the PMCMRplus package in R and scikit-posthocs in Python; they give the same p-values. Printing PMCMRplus’s result shows any p-value below 2 × 10⁻¹⁶ only as “<2e-16”, so print its $p.value table to see them.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: After Cochran’s Q: pairwise McNemar tests
text:
After Cochran’s Q: pairwise McNemar tests
After Cochran’s Q, compare pairs of visits with McNemar’s test and adjust with Holm. Page 9 found that walking-aid use changed over the year in 328 patients assessed at all four visits:

RPython



aid <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(walking_aid))) |>               # patients assessed at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = walking_aid)

visit_pairs <- combn(c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"), 2)    # six pairs, one per column
mcnemar_p <- apply(visit_pairs, 2, function(pair) {
  mcnemar.test(table(factor(aid[[pair[1]]], levels = 0:1), factor(aid[[pair[2]]], levels = 0:1)))$p.value
})
mcnemar_results <- tibble(first = visit_pairs[1, ], second = visit_pairs[2, ],
                          p = mcnemar_p, p_holm = p.adjust(mcnemar_p, method = "holm"))
mcnemar_results

  first second        p   p_holm
  <chr> <chr>     <dbl>    <dbl>

aid = proms.pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="walking_aid").dropna()   # assessed at all four visits

mcnemar_p = []
visit_pairs = list(itertools.combinations(["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"], 2))

Tip🔀 R vs Python: pairwise log-rank tests



lifelines has pairwise_logrank_test(), which runs every pair at once and leaves the adjustment to you. lifelines’ Cox model stops iterating slightly early by default, so, as on page 14, the Python Cox fit passes fit_options={"precision": 1e-12} to match R’s hazard ratios. title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: Do you need a significant overall test first?
text:
Do you need a significant overall test first?
A common rule says: only run post-hoc tests if the overall test (the ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis or chi-square) is significant. It comes from Fisher’s least significant difference method, which runs unadjusted pairwise tests and relies on the overall test as a gate. That gate only fully protects you with three groups.
The tests on this page don’t need the gate. Tukey’s HSD and Games-Howell control the family-wise error rate on their own, and so do Dunn’s test and any other set of pairwise tests once Holm’s adjustment is applied. Requiring a significant overall test first just makes them stricter than they need to be.
The two kinds of test can also disagree, and that’s not a contradiction: - A significant overall test with no significant pair, as with complications by ASA class above (overall p = 0.016; no pair below 0.05 after adjustment). The overall test pools the evidence from all four classes, while each pair uses only two of them, and the ASA 1 and ASA 4 groups are small. Report it as it is: complication rates differed across ASA classes overall, but no single pair of classes differed clearly. - A significant pair with no significant overall test. This can happen when one pair differs and the others don’t, diluting the overall test.
What to do: 1. Decide before you look at the data which comparisons you’ll make: every pair, or a few planned ones. 2. If your question is about pairs, go straight to an adjusted pairwise method. The overall test is optional; report it if your readers expect it. 3. Never run unadjusted pairwise tests you didn’t plan, whatever the overall test says. 4. Say what you did in the Methods.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: Planned comparisons and how to report them
text:
Planned comparisons and how to report them
Not every comparison is a fishing trip. A study comparing a new implant with the standard one has one pre-specified comparison, named in the protocol before any data were collected. It needs no adjustment, because it isn’t one of many. If you planned three comparisons, adjust for three, not for every possible pair.
Everything else is exploratory: comparisons chosen after seeing the data, or a scan across many outcomes. Adjust for every comparison you looked at, not only the ones you report, and label the results exploratory: they suggest questions for the next study, not conclusions.

Methods: Pairwise comparisons after the omnibus tests used Tukey’s honestly significant difference test (after ANOVA), Dunn’s test (after Kruskal-Wallis) and Fisher’s exact tests (after chi-square), with Holm’s adjustment for multiple comparisons where the method did not adjust itself. All pairwise comparisons were exploratory.
Results: Across ASA classes, one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 596) = 23.9 (p < 0.001); in pairwise comparisons, the difference in mean age between ASA 3 and ASA 2 was 5.0 years (95% CI 3.0 to 6.9; p < 0.001). Table 2 gives all six pairwise comparisons.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: report every comparison you ran



Running ten comparisons and reporting the two significant ones hides how many chances you had. Give the number of comparisons and the adjustment in the Methods, and put the full set of pairwise results in a table or supplement.

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
text: Before a measurement goes into a study, someone should ask: if it were measured again, would you get the same answer? Alignment angles on long-leg radiographs are a good example. Before an osteotomy around the knee, the surgeon works out the correction from the hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), the medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) and the lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), so an error in the reading becomes an error in the correction. Two surgeons can place the same landmarks a little differently, and one surgeon can place them differently on another day. This page shows how to measure that, using the practice data’s reliability study: 60 knees, each measured by two raters (R1 and R2), twice, at least two weeks apart.

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
text:
Reliability or agreement?
The two words are often used as if they meant the same thing. They don’t: - Reliability asks whether a measurement can tell patients apart: are the real differences between knees large compared with the disagreement between readings? It’s measured with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), a number from 0 to 1. Because it compares the disagreement with how much the knees differ, the same raters look more reliable in a cohort with a wider range of deformities. - Agreement asks how close two readings are, in the measurement’s own units. If rater 2 reads every knee 3° higher than rater 1, that’s poor agreement, even though the two raters put the knees in exactly the same order. It’s measured with the Bland-Altman limits of agreement, in degrees.
Report both. A surgeon planning an osteotomy needs to know the agreement in degrees, not only that the ICC was 0.9.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

readings <- read_csv("data/radiographic_reliability.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
text:
The intraclass correlation coefficient
There are several ICCs, and the right one depends on the design. Three choices define it (Koo & Li, 2016): - Model: are the raters a random sample of the raters who might use this measurement (two-way random), or the only raters you care about (two-way mixed)? For a measurement other surgeons will use, choose random. - Type: should a rater who always reads higher count against the measurement (absolute agreement) or not (consistency)? For angles that feed clinical decisions, it should: choose absolute agreement. - Unit: will the study use one rater’s reading (single) or the average of several (average)? Usually single.
For inter-rater reliability of HKA, that gives a two-way random, absolute-agreement, single-rater ICC, written ICC(A,1) (or ICC(2,1) in Shrout and Fleiss’s older naming). Using each rater’s first-session readings:

RPython



inter_hka <- readings |>
  filter(session == 1) |>
  select(knee_id, rater, hka_deg) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rater, values_from = hka_deg)     # one column per rater

inter_icc <- irr::icc(inter_hka[, c("R1", "R2")], model = "twoway", type = "agreement", unit = "single")
inter_icc

 Single Score Intraclass Correlation

   Model: twoway 
   Type : agreement 

   Subjects = 60 
     Raters = 2 
   ICC(A,1) = 0.889

 F-Test, H0: r0 = 0 ; H1: r0 > 0 
   F(59,59) = 18.3 , p = 8.19e-23 

 95%-Confidence Interval for ICC Population Values:
  0.816 < ICC < 0.934





first_session = readings[readings["session"] == 1]
inter_icc = pg.intraclass_corr(data=first_session, targets="knee_id", raters="rater", ratings="hka_deg")
print(inter_icc[["Type", "ICC", "CI95"]])     # ICC(A,1): two-way random, absolute agreement, single rater

       Type       ICC          CI95
0  ICC(1,1)  0.888950  [0.82, 0.93]
1  ICC(A,1)  0.889383  [0.82, 0.93]
2  ICC(C,1)  0.896386  [0.83, 0.94]
3  ICC(1,k)  0.941211   [0.9, 0.96]
4  ICC(A,k)  0.941454   [0.9, 0.97]
5  ICC(C,k)  0.945362  [0.91, 0.97]






ICC(A,1) = 0.889 (Python’s ICC(A,1) row; R prints 0.889).
95% CI 0.82 to 0.93. Koo and Li’s guide: below 0.5 poor, 0.5 to 0.75 moderate, 0.75 to 0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent. Judge by the CI, not the point estimate: this one runs from good to excellent.
The F test (R) tests whether the ICC is above 0. It nearly always is, so it’s rarely worth reporting.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: always say which ICC



The same data give a different ICC for every model, type and unit: here 0.889 for absolute agreement and 0.896 for consistency, and 0.94 for the average of the two raters. “ICC = 0.94” with no form named can’t be interpreted. Write the form out in the Methods.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: one ICC or all of them



R’s irr::icc() computes the one ICC you ask for. pingouin’s intraclass_corr() computes all six forms at once; pick the row. It labels them two ways: ICC(A,1) in McGraw and Wong’s naming, which matches R’s arguments, or ICC2 in older pingouin versions. pingouin rounds the CI to 2 decimals.

text:
Inter-rater and intra-rater reliability
The ICC above is inter-rater reliability: two raters, same films. Intra-rater (test-retest) reliability uses one rater reading the same films twice, far enough apart that they don’t remember their first answers. The same ICC form applies, with the two sessions in place of the two raters:

  filter(rater == "R1") |>

  pivot_wider(names_from = session, values_from = hka_deg, names_prefix = "session_")

intra_icc <- irr::icc(intra_hka[, c("session_1", "session_2")], model = "twoway", type = "agreement", unit = "single")

  0.862 < ICC < 0.948

intra_icc = pg.intraclass_corr(data=rater_1, targets="knee_id", raters="session", ratings="hka_deg")
print(intra_icc.set_index("Type").loc["ICC(A,1)", ["ICC", "CI95"]])

ICC         0.914844
CI95    [0.86, 0.95]
Name: ICC(A,1), dtype: object





Rater 1 agreed with themselves a little better than with rater 2: intra-rater ICC(A,1) = 0.915 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.95), excellent at its point estimate and good to excellent across its CI.

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
section: Bland-Altman: how far apart are the readings?
text:
Bland-Altman: how far apart are the readings?
The ICC is a ratio and has no units. To see how far apart two readings can be, in degrees, plot the difference between them against their mean, one point per knee. Then add three lines: - The bias: the mean difference, showing whether one rater reads systematically higher. - The 95% limits of agreement: bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences. For 95% of knees, rater 2’s reading will fall between these limits relative to rater 1’s.

RPython



inter_hka <- inter_hka |> mutate(difference = R2 - R1, mean = (R1 + R2) / 2)

n_knees <- nrow(inter_hka)
bias <- mean(inter_hka$difference)
sd_diff <- sd(inter_hka$difference)
limits <- bias + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sd_diff
se_limit <- sqrt(3 * sd_diff^2 / n_knees)                      # Bland and Altman's SE for each limit
limit_cis <- rbind(lower = limits[1] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n_knees - 1) * se_limit,
                   upper = limits[2] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n_knees - 1) * se_limit)

bias_ci <- t.test(inter_hka$difference)$conf.int                # the CI of the mean difference
c(bias = bias, bias_ci = bias_ci, sd = sd_diff, limits = limits)

bias = difference.mean()
sd_diff = difference.std()                                     # pandas uses n - 1, like R
limits = bias + np.array([-1.96, 1.96]) * sd_diff
se_limit = np.sqrt(3 * sd_diff**2 / n_knees)                   # Bland and Altman's SE for each limit
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n_knees - 1)
bias_ci = stats.ttest_1samp(difference, 0).confidence_interval()
print(round(bias, 3), round(float(bias_ci.low), 3), round(float(bias_ci.high), 3), round(sd_diff, 3), limits.round(3))

0.503 0.076 0.93 1.654 [-2.738  3.744]

print((limits - t_crit * se_limit).round(3), (limits + t_crit * se_limit).round(3))   # CI of each limit: lower ends, upper ends

[-3.477  3.004] [-1.998  4.484]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(mean, difference)
ax.axhline(bias)
for limit in limits:
    ax.axhline(limit, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean of the two readings (°)")
ax.set_ylabel("Rater 2 − rater 1 (°)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()












Bias = 0.50° (95% CI 0.08° to 0.93°): rater 2 reads half a degree higher than rater 1 on average, the same difference page 7’s exercise 2 found with a paired t test.
Limits of agreement, −2.74° to 3.74°: for 95% of knees, rater 2’s reading will be between 2.7° below and 3.7° above rater 1’s.
The CIs of the limits (−3.48° to −2.00° and 3.00° to 4.48°) show how precisely 60 knees pin the limits down.
The plot: the points scatter evenly around the bias line, with no trend up or down as the mean angle changes. A trend would mean the raters disagree more for some knees (more varus, say) than others, and a single pair of limits wouldn’t describe them.

Whether limits of ±3.7° are good enough is a clinical question, not a statistical one. If a 3° difference would change the planned correction in your study, it matters. Decide the acceptable limits before you run the reliability study, and compare the limits (and their CIs) with them.

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
text:
Kappa for categories
For a category, like CPAK class, use Cohen’s kappa: the agreement between two raters beyond what chance alone would produce. Kappa is 1 for perfect agreement and 0 for agreement no better than chance.

RPython



cpak_levels <- c("I", "II", "III", "IV", "V", "VI", "VII", "VIII", "IX")
cpak <- readings |>
  filter(session == 1) |>
  select(knee_id, rater, cpak_class) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rater, values_from = cpak_class) |>
  mutate(R1 = factor(R1, levels = cpak_levels), R2 = factor(R2, levels = cpak_levels))

mean(cpak$R1 == cpak$R2)                                     # simple percentage agreement

[1] 0.6666667

cpak_kappa <- DescTools::CohenKappa(cpak$R1, cpak$R2, conf.level = 0.95)
cpak_kappa

    kappa    lwr.ci    upr.ci 
0.5830438 0.4352380 0.7308495 





cpak_levels = ["I", "II", "III", "IV", "V", "VI", "VII", "VIII", "IX"]
cpak = first_session.pivot(index="knee_id", columns="rater", values="cpak_class")
print((cpak["R1"] == cpak["R2"]).mean())                       # simple percentage agreement

0.6666666666666666

cpak_table = pd.crosstab(pd.Categorical(cpak["R1"], categories=cpak_levels),
                         pd.Categorical(cpak["R2"], categories=cpak_levels), dropna=False)
cpak_kappa = cohens_kappa(cpak_table.to_numpy())
print(cpak_kappa.kappa, cpak_kappa.kappa_low, cpak_kappa.kappa_upp)

0.5830437804030576 0.4352380334984082 0.7308495273077069





The raters gave the same CPAK class to 40 of the 60 knees (66.7%), but some of that would happen by chance. Kappa = 0.58 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.73): moderate agreement at its point estimate on Landis and Koch’s scale (0.41 to 0.60 moderate, 0.61 to 0.80 substantial, above 0.80 almost perfect). As with the ICC, judge it by the CI: moderate to substantial.
Weighted kappa for ordered categories. Plain kappa treats every disagreement as equally bad. When the categories have an order, a near miss should count less than a big miss. CPAK class has no single order (it’s a 3 × 3 grid of two angles), but each axis does. The arithmetic HKA group goes varus, neutral, valgus. A weighted kappa gives a disagreement between varus and neutral half the penalty of one between varus and valgus (linear weights):

RPython



hka_group <- function(cpak_class) {
  # CPAK classes I-III, IV-VI and VII-IX each run varus, neutral, valgus
  factor(c("varus", "neutral", "valgus")[(as.integer(cpak_class) - 1) %% 3 + 1],
         levels = c("varus", "neutral", "valgus"))                # in order
}
hka_table <- table(R1 = hka_group(cpak$R1), R2 = hka_group(cpak$R2))
hka_table

         R2
R1        varus neutral valgus
  varus      16       4      0
  neutral     5      23      1
  valgus      0       2      9

unweighted_kappa <- DescTools::CohenKappa(hka_table, conf.level = 0.95)                            # unweighted
weighted_kappa <- DescTools::CohenKappa(hka_table, weights = "Equal-Spacing", conf.level = 0.95)   # linear weights
rbind(unweighted = unweighted_kappa, weighted = weighted_kappa)

               kappa    lwr.ci    upr.ci
unweighted 0.6769852 0.5098602 0.8441102
weighted   0.7293233 0.5843821 0.8742645





hka_group = {cls: ["varus", "neutral", "valgus"][i % 3] for i, cls in enumerate(cpak_levels)}   # I-III, IV-VI, VII-IX
order = ["varus", "neutral", "valgus"]
hka_table = pd.crosstab(pd.Categorical(cpak["R1"].map(hka_group), categories=order),
                        pd.Categorical(cpak["R2"].map(hka_group), categories=order), dropna=False)
print(hka_table)

col_0    varus  neutral  valgus
row_0                          
varus       16        4       0
neutral      5       23       1
valgus       0        2       9

unweighted = cohens_kappa(hka_table.to_numpy())
weighted = cohens_kappa(hka_table.to_numpy(), wt="linear")     # linear weights
print(unweighted.kappa, weighted.kappa, weighted.kappa_low, weighted.kappa_upp)

0.6769851951547781 0.7293233082706767 0.5843821108979698 0.8742645056433836





The raters agreed on the HKA group for 48 of 60 knees, and every disagreement was a near miss: no knee was called varus by one rater and valgus by the other. Unweighted kappa is 0.68; the weighted kappa, which gives near misses partial credit, is 0.73 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.87): substantial at its point estimate, moderate to almost perfect across its CI.






Warning⚠️ Watch out: weighted kappa needs the categories in order



The weights depend on the order of the categories. Put them in their real order (varus, neutral, valgus) yourself. Some functions sort categories alphabetically, which would put “neutral” before “valgus” before “varus” and weight the wrong disagreements: irr::kappa2(weight = "equal") does, and gives 0.63 here instead of 0.73. Never use weighted kappa for categories with no order, like CPAK class itself.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: kappa and its CI



DescTools’ CohenKappa() and statsmodels’ cohens_kappa() give the same kappa and the same CI. DescTools calls linear weights “Equal-Spacing” and quadratic weights “Fleiss-Cohen”; statsmodels uses wt="linear" and wt="quadratic". scikit-learn’s cohen_kappa_score() gives the kappa but no CI, and for weighted kappa it sorts the categories alphabetically unless you pass them in order with labels=.

title: 17 · Agreement & reliability
text:
How to report it

Methods: Two raters measured the hip-knee-ankle angle, MPTA and LDFA on 60 long-leg radiographs used for osteotomy planning, twice, at least 2 weeks apart. Inter- and intra-rater reliability were assessed with two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, single-rater intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC(A,1)) and interpreted according to Koo and Li. Inter-rater reliability used each rater’s first reading; intra-rater reliability compared rater 1’s two readings. Agreement was assessed with Bland-Altman 95% limits of agreement. Agreement on CPAK class was assessed with Cohen’s kappa, and on the ordered arithmetic HKA group with linearly weighted kappa.
Results: For the hip-knee-ankle angle, the inter-rater ICC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.93) and rater 1’s intra-rater ICC 0.91 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.95). The mean difference between rater 2 and rater 1 was 0.50° (95% CI 0.08° to 0.93°), with 95% limits of agreement from −2.74° (95% CI −3.48° to −2.00°) to 3.74° (95% CI 3.00° to 4.48°). For CPAK class, κ = 0.58 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.73); for the arithmetic HKA group, weighted κ = 0.73 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.87).

3. A colleague reports that the two raters’ HKA readings correlate well (Pearson’s r = 0.90, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.94) as evidence that they agree. What’s wrong with that? Show it by adding 5° to every one of rater 2’s readings and recalculating r and the ICC.

title: Welchen statistischen Test soll ich verwenden?
text:
Suchen Sie Ihr Ziel in der linken Spalte (zum Beispiel zwei unabhängige Gruppen vergleichen).
Suchen Sie Ihren Datentyp in der obersten Zeile. Sie sind nicht sicher, ob Ihre Messwerte normalverteilt (Gauss-verteilt) sind? Lesen Sie zuerst Verteilungen und Testwahl.
Klicken Sie auf den Test.
Sie kennen den Namen des Tests bereits? Schlagen Sie ihn unter Tests A–Z nach.
Nach Harvey Motulsky, Intuitive Biostatistics (Oxford University Press), und dem GraphPad Statistics Guide.

title: Tests A–Z
text:
Sie kennen den Namen des Tests, den Sie brauchen? Suchen Sie ihn hier und springen Sie direkt zu seinem Abschnitt. Publikationen nennen denselben Test oft unterschiedlich, deshalb haben diese Namen eigene Zeilen. Die Tabelle ist nach dem unterscheidenden Namen sortiert: Fisher unter F, Wilcoxon unter W, die t-Tests unter t. Sie wissen nicht, welcher Test zu Ihrer Frage passt? Beginnen Sie mit Welchen statistischen Test soll ich verwenden?



Test oder Methode
Verwenden, um
Wo

Dasselbe wie die kumulative Inzidenz

Eine Messgrösse zwischen drei oder mehr unabhängigen Gruppen vergleichen

Eine Messgrösse über drei oder mehr Kontrollen oder gematchte Bedingungen hinweg vergleichen

Eine Ja/Nein-Zielgrösse in einer Gruppe beschreiben

Dasselbe wie die stratifizierte Cox-Regression

Das Überleben innerhalb gematchter Gruppen vergleichen oder bei Patientinnen und Patienten, die auf beiden Seiten operiert wurden

Wie der t-Test für unabhängige Stichproben, setzt aber gleiche Streuungen voraus; verwenden Sie stattdessen den t-Test nach Welch

Den Mittelwert einer Gruppe mit einem hypothetischen Wert vergleichen

Eine Messgrösse zwischen zwei gepaarten Messungen vergleichen, zum Beispiel vor und nach der Operation

Eine Messgrösse zwischen zwei unabhängigen Gruppen vergleichen

Dasselbe wie der t-Test für unabhängige Stichproben auf dieser Website

Siehe nichtparametrische Regression

title: Installieren & einrichten
text: Das dauert beim ersten Mal 30–45 Minuten, und Sie machen es nur einmal pro Computer. Gehen Sie die Schritte der Reihe nach durch. Jeder Schritt endet mit einer kurzen Prüfung.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
1. R installieren

Öffnen Sie https://cloud.r-project.org.
Klicken Sie auf Download R for macOS oder Download R for Windows.

Mac: Wählen Sie das Installationsprogramm für Ihren Chip. Apple-Menü → Über diesen Mac (About This Mac): «Apple M…» bedeutet Apple silicon (arm64), «Intel» bedeutet Intel (x86_64).
Windows: Klicken Sie auf base und dann auf den Download-Link oben auf der Seite.

Öffnen Sie die heruntergeladene Datei und übernehmen Sie die Standardeinstellungen.

Prüfung: Positron findet R in Schritt 4. Auf einem Mac können Sie auch das Terminal öffnen und R --version eingeben.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
2. uv und Python installieren
Mac: Öffnen Sie das Terminal und führen Sie aus:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Windows: Öffnen Sie PowerShell und führen Sie aus:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Schliessen Sie das Fenster, öffnen Sie ein neues und installieren Sie Python:
uv python install 3.13
Prüfung: uv --version gibt eine Versionsnummer aus.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
3. Git installieren

Mac: Führen Sie im Terminal xcode-select --install aus und klicken Sie auf Installieren (Install). Das installiert die Kommandozeilen-Werkzeuge von Apple, zu denen Git gehört.
Windows: Laden Sie Git von https://git-scm.com/downloads herunter und übernehmen Sie die Standardeinstellungen.

Prüfung: git --version gibt eine Versionsnummer aus.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
4. Positron installieren
Laden Sie Positron von https://positron.posit.co herunter und installieren Sie es wie jede andere App. Positron führt R und Python nebeneinander aus. Möchten Sie lieber RStudio oder VS Code verwenden? Siehe Andere Editoren.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
5. Dieses Repository herunterladen
Legen Sie im Terminal (Mac) oder in PowerShell (Windows) einen Ordner projects an und laden Sie das Repository («klonen») in diesen Ordner herunter:
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation.git
Verwenden Sie einen Ordner, der nicht mit der Cloud synchronisiert wird. Documents und Desktop werden oft von iCloud (Mac) oder OneDrive (Windows) synchronisiert. Die Synchronisierung verlangsamt die R- und Python-Umgebungen, die die Schritte 6 und 7 anlegen, und kann sie beschädigen.
Wählen Sie dann in Positron File → Open Folder… und öffnen Sie stats-formation.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
6. Die R-Packages installieren
Starten Sie in Positron eine R-Konsole: Wählen Sie in der Sprachauswahl oben rechts im Bereich Console die Option R. Weil R im Repository-Ordner startet, schaltet es die Package-Liste dieses Projekts ein. Führen Sie dann aus:
renv::restore()
Antworten Sie mit Y, wenn Sie gefragt werden. Das installiert jedes R-Package, das die Tutorials verwenden, in genau den Versionen, die wir getestet haben. Es dauert einige Minuten.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
7. Die Python-Packages installieren
Öffnen Sie das Terminal von Positron (Terminal → New Terminal). Es öffnet sich im Repository-Ordner. Führen Sie aus:
uv sync
Das legt im Ordner .venv eine eigene Python-Umgebung mit jedem Package an, das die Tutorials verwenden. Sagen Sie Positron dann, dass es diese verwenden soll: Wählen Sie in der Sprachauswahl im Bereich Console das Python, dessen Pfad .venv enthält.

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
8. Prüfen, ob alles funktioniert
Führen Sie im Terminal von Positron beide Prüfungen aus:
Rscript scripts/check_setup.R
uv run python scripts/check_setup.py
Jede Prüfung endet mit All good - you are ready. Steht in einer Zeile PROBLEM, sagt sie Ihnen, was zu tun ist. Beheben Sie das Problem und führen Sie die Prüfung erneut aus.
Wenn unter Windows Rscript «not recognized» meldet, führen Sie die R-Prüfung stattdessen in der R-Konsole von Positron aus:
source("scripts/check_setup.R")

title: Installieren & einrichten
text:
Die Daten ohne Klonen lesen
Sie können Schritt 5 (Klonen) überspringen und die Übungsdaten direkt von GitHub lesen. Die Packages brauchen Sie weiterhin; installieren Sie diese zuerst.

RPython


install.packages(c("readr", "readxl"))   # einmalig

cohort <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/cohort.csv")


Starten Sie Python mit den Packages, die es braucht. In einem Terminal:
uv run --with pandas --with openpyxl python
Dann:
import pandas as pd

cohort = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/cohort.csv")



Jede CSV-Datei funktioniert auf dieselbe Weise. Ersetzen Sie in jedem Beispiel "data/" durch "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/".
Excel-Dateien sind anders. read_excel() in R kann keine Webadresse lesen, laden Sie die Datei deshalb zuerst herunter. pd.read_excel() in Python kann die Adresse direkt lesen.

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(url, path, mode = "wb")   # "wb" hält die Datei unter Windows unversehrt
site_a <- readxl::read_excel(path, sheet = "Site A")

Andere Editoren

title: 1 · Aufgeräumte Daten (Tidy Data)
text: In einem Forschungsprojekt geht die meiste Zeit dafür drauf, die Daten in Form zu bringen, nicht für die Statistik. Fehler, die hier passieren, sind die gefährliche Sorte: Der Code läuft, die Tabellen sehen gut aus, und die Zahlen sind trotzdem falsch. Diese Seite zeigt, wie Sie Daten so erheben, dass sie sauber ankommen, wie Sie sie aufräumen, wenn sie es nicht tun, und wie Sie belegen, dass Ihr Aufräumen nichts verändert hat, was es nicht hätte verändern dürfen.

title: 1 · Aufgeräumte Daten (Tidy Data)
text:
Was aufgeräumte Daten bedeuten
Daten sind aufgeräumt (tidy), wenn:

jede Variable eine Spalte ist,
jede Beobachtung eine Zeile ist und
jede Art von Beobachtungseinheit ihre eigene Tabelle hat.







Hinweis💡 Einfach erklärt



Eine Angabe pro Zelle, eine Beobachtung pro Zeile, und nie zwei Arten von Zeilen in derselben Tabelle. Eine Tabelle, die für Menschen leicht zu lesen ist, lässt sich oft schlecht mit dem Computer auswerten, und umgekehrt. Statistiksoftware braucht die zweite Art.


Hier ein typisches Beispiel für ein nicht aufgeräumtes Tabellenblatt mit PROM-Scores (PROM: patientenberichtetes Messinstrument): eine Zeile pro Patientin oder Patient und eine Spalte für jede Kontrolle. Die Kontrolle ist eine Variable, steckt aber in den Spaltennamen.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

wide <- tibble(
  case_id = c("C0001", "C0002", "C0003"),
  preop   = c(41.2, 55.0, 38.7),
  `6wk`   = c(60.1, NA,   58.3),
  `1yr`   = c(88.0, 92.4, 79.5)
)
wide

# Aufgeräumt: eine Zeile pro Fall und Kontrolle
long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(-case_id, names_to = "visit", values_to = "prom_score")

title: 1 · Aufgeräumte Daten (Tidy Data)
text:
Aufgeräumte Daten erheben
Am billigsten ist das Aufräumen, das gar nicht nötig wird. Bevor jemand auch nur aus einer Krankengeschichte Daten erhebt, schreiben Sie das Datenwörterbuch: Name, Bedeutung, Typ, Einheit und erlaubte Werte jeder Variable. Danach bauen Sie das Datenerhebungsblatt aus dem Datenwörterbuch.
Diese Website enthält eine vorbereitete Vorlage, die Sie kopieren können: templates/data-collection-template.xlsx. Sie hat vier Tabellenblätter:

README — die Regeln unten, für alle, die Daten aus den Krankengeschichten erheben.
data — eine Kopfzeile, und bei jeder Spalte ausser der Studien-ID Dropdown-Listen oder Wertebereichsprüfungen, damit keine Tippfehler hineingelangen.
dictionary — was jede Spalte bedeutet.
missing_codes — was genau einzutragen ist, wenn ein Wert in der Krankengeschichte fehlt.

Die Regeln, die die Vorlage durchsetzt:

Eine Zeile pro Eingriff, eine Spalte pro Variable, ein Wert pro Zelle.
Eine Studien-ID (der Studiencode), nie die Patientennummer oder der Name. Der Schlüssel, der die Studiencodes den Patientennummern zuordnet, liegt in einer eigenen, gesicherten Datei. Er wird von der Person aufbewahrt, die im Gesuch an die Ethikkommission dafür benannt ist und nicht am Projekt mitarbeitet.
Kategorien nur aus Dropdown-Listen (nicht F neben female).
Zahlen nur in Zahlenspalten; die Einheiten stehen im Datenwörterbuch.
Echte Datumsangaben, kein Text.
Fehlend heisst: Dropdown-Eintrag «Not recorded» oder eine leere Zahlen- bzw. Datumszelle.
Keine Farben, keine Fettschrift, keine Kommentare, keine verbundenen Zellen, keine Titelzeilen und keine Summenzeilen.

Das Blatt «dictionary» lesen Sie wie alle anderen Daten ein:

RPython



library(readxl)

dictionary <- read_excel("templates/data-collection-template.xlsx", sheet = "dictionary")

title: 1 · Aufgeräumte Daten (Tidy Data)
text:
Eine unordentliche Arbeitsmappe aufräumen
Echte Erhebungstabellen halten sich selten an diese Regeln. data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx bildet die Probleme nach, die wir in echten Erhebungstabellen sehen. Öffnen Sie die Datei in Excel und sehen Sie sie an, bevor Sie Code ausführen:

zwei Reiter, Site A und Site B, deren Spalten nicht übereinstimmen (Site B hat in der Mitte eine zusätzliche Spalte MUA)
zwei Kopfzeilen oberhalb der Tabelle (Banner-Zeilen) und eine Zeile mit verbundenen Gruppenüberschriften über der eigentlichen Kopfzeile
eine Zeile TOTAL am Ende jedes Reiters
zwei Spalten Date und zwei Spalten Score (präoperativer PROM-Score und PROM-Score nach 1 Jahr)
gemischte Datumsformate, Einheiten in Zahlenzellen, ASA-Klassen in römischen Ziffern, fünf Schreibweisen für «fehlend»
Revisionen, die nur durch eine rote Füllung der Zelle mit der Studien-ID markiert sind
doppelte Zeilen

Wir beheben die Probleme Schritt für Schritt. Jeder Schritt ist klein genug, um ihn zu prüfen. Führen Sie die Schritte der Reihe nach aus: Jeder beginnt mit dem Resultat des vorigen.

Schritt 1: beide Reiter als Text einlesen
Lesen Sie zuerst alles als Text ein. Wenn die Software die Typen errät, macht sie aus 32.1 kg/m2 stillschweigend einen fehlenden Wert, und Sie bemerken es nie. Die Typen wandeln wir in Schritt 5 gezielt um.

RPython



path <- "data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"

read_site <- function(sheet) {
  # skip = 3 überspringt die zwei Banner-Zeilen und die Zeile mit den Gruppenüberschriften
  raw <- read_excel(path, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, col_types = "text",
                    .name_repair = "minimal")
  names(raw) <- str_trim(names(raw))   # «Study ID » hat auf Site B ein Leerzeichen am Ende

  # Die zwei Paare Date/Score: laut Gruppenüberschrift zuerst präoperativ, dann 1 Jahr
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Date"]  <- c("prom_preop_date", "prom_1yr_date")
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Score"] <- c("prom_preop", "prom_1yr")

  raw |>
    janitor::clean_names() |> # «Pt Name» -> pt_name, «Study ID» -> study_id
    mutate(site = sheet)      # merken, aus welchem Reiter jede Zeile stammt
}

raw <- bind_rows(read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B"))   # ordnet die Spalten nach Namen zu
nrow(raw)

[1] 126

names(raw)

 [1] "pt_name"         "mrn"             "study_id"        "dos"            
 [5] "age"             "sex"             "bmi"             "asa"            
 [9] "comorbidities"   "procedure"       "los"             "prom_preop_date"
[13] "prom_preop"      "prom_1yr_date"   "prom_1yr"        "notes"          
[17] "site"            "mua"            





import re

path = "data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"

def read_site(sheet):
    # header=3 nimmt die 4. Zeile als Spaltennamen (nach Bannern und Gruppenüberschriften)
    raw = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet, header=3, dtype=str)
    names = [str(c).strip() for c in raw.columns]   # «Study ID » hat auf Site B ein Leerzeichen am Ende

    # pandas benennt wiederholte Spaltenköpfe in «Date.1» und «Score.1» um
    pairs = {"Date": "prom_preop_date", "Score": "prom_preop",
             "Date.1": "prom_1yr_date", "Score.1": "prom_1yr"}
    names = [pairs.get(n, n) for n in names]

    # «Pt Name» -> pt_name, «Study ID» -> study_id
    raw.columns = [re.sub(r"[^0-9a-z]+", "_", n.lower()).strip("_") for n in names]
    return raw.assign(site=sheet)   # merken, aus welchem Reiter jede Zeile stammt

raw = pd.concat([read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B")], ignore_index=True)  # ordnet nach Namen zu
print(len(raw))

126

print(list(raw.columns))

['pt_name', 'mrn', 'study_id', 'dos', 'age', 'sex', 'bmi', 'asa', 'comorbidities', 'procedure', 'los', 'prom_preop_date', 'prom_preop', 'prom_1yr_date', 'prom_1yr', 'notes', 'site', 'mua']





126 Zeilen: 60 Patientinnen und Patienten pro Reiter, dazu in jedem je 2 Duplikate und eine Summenzeile. Weil wir die Reiter nach Spaltennamen untereinander gestellt haben, hat die zusätzliche Spalte MUA von Site B nichts verschoben. Bei den Zeilen von Site A fehlt mua einfach. Wären die Zellen nach Position kopiert worden, stünden die LOS-Werte unter der falschen Überschrift.
In R rufen wir janitor::clean_names() mit dem Package-Namen davor auf, statt janitor mit library() zu laden. Beim Laden von janitor werden die eigenen Funktionen chisq.test() und fisher.test() von R durch die Versionen aus janitor überdeckt. Bei gewöhnlichen Tabellen geben sie dieselben Antworten, aber die Meldung über das Überdecken verwirrt, und es wird schwerer zu erkennen, welche Funktion Sie tatsächlich aufrufen.






Tipp🔀 R oder Python: dieselbe Excel-Datei, anders eingelesen




Wiederholte Spaltenköpfe. R (mit .name_repair = "minimal") behält beide Date-Spalten als Date. pandas benennt die zweite in Date.1 um.
Echte Excel-Datumsangaben. Als Text eingelesen, liefert R die Excel-Seriennummer (42010 bedeutet 6. Januar 2015). pandas liefert 2015-01-06 00:00:00. Schritt 5 behandelt beide.





Schritt 2: Zeilen und Spalten entfernen, die keine Daten sind

RPython



step2 <- raw |>
  filter(is.na(pt_name) | pt_name != "TOTAL") |>   # die Summenzeilen
  distinct() |>                                      # exakt doppelte Zeilen
  select(-pt_name, -mrn, -mua)                       # Identifikatoren und eine Spalte, die wir nicht brauchen

nrow(step2)

[1] 120





step2 = (raw[raw["pt_name"] != "TOTAL"]           # die Summenzeilen
         .drop_duplicates()                        # exakt doppelte Zeilen
         .drop(columns=["pt_name", "mrn", "mua"])) # Identifikatoren und eine Spalte, die wir nicht brauchen
print(len(step2))

120





Namen und MRN entfernen Sie so früh wie möglich. Alles ab hier arbeitet nur noch mit einer Studien-ID.


Schritt 3: eine einzige Art, «fehlend» zu sagen

RPython



missing_codes <- c("N/A", "unk", "-", "999")

step3 <- step2 |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) if_else(x %in% missing_codes, NA, x)))

# Wie viele BMI-Werte fehlen jetzt?
sum(is.na(step3$bmi))

[1] 8





missing_codes = ["N/A", "unk", "-", "999"]

step3 = step2.replace(missing_codes, pd.NA)

# Wie viele BMI-Werte fehlen jetzt?
print(step3["bmi"].isna().sum())

8











Warnung⚠️ Achtung: 999 ist nur dann ein Code für fehlende Werte, wenn Ihr Datenwörterbuch das so festlegt



In diesem Tabellenblatt bedeutet 999 in Zahlenspalten «fehlend». In einem anderen Blatt kann es ein echter Wert sein. Tragen Sie jeden Code für fehlende Werte ins Datenwörterbuch ein, bevor die Erhebung beginnt.




Schritt 4: die farbig markierten Revisionen wiederherstellen
Das Blatt markiert revidierte Fälle nur mit einer roten Füllung der Zelle mit der Studien-ID. Die meiste Software, die eine Tabelle einliest, sieht Farben gar nicht. Genau deshalb darf Farbe nie Daten tragen. Hier müssen wir sie mühsam herausholen.

RPython



library(tidyxl)

cells   <- xlsx_cells(path)                                 # eine Zeile pro Tabellenzelle
fills   <- xlsx_formats(path)$local$fill$patternFill$fgColor$rgb  # Füllfarbe jedes Formats

revised_ids <- cells |>
  filter(fills[local_format_id] %in% "FFFF9999") |>         # die rote Füllung
  pull(character) |>
  str_trim() |>
  unique()

length(revised_ids)

[1] 18





import openpyxl

workbook = openpyxl.load_workbook(path)

revised_ids = set()
for sheet in workbook.worksheets:
    for row in sheet.iter_rows(min_row=5):        # die Daten beginnen in Zeile 5
        for cell in row:
            if cell.fill.fgColor.rgb == "FFFF9999":   # die rote Füllung
                revised_ids.add(str(cell.value).strip())

print(len(revised_ids))

Die Spalte Notes erwähnt einige Revisionen («revised 2021 for loosening»), aber nicht alle. Hätten wir uns auf die Notizen verlassen, wären uns Fälle entgangen. Nur die Farben waren vollständig.


Schritt 5: jeder Spalte ihren richtigen Typ geben
Nun wandeln wir jede Textspalte in das um, was sie wirklich ist. Eine kleine Funktion kümmert sich um die gemischten Datumsformate. Jede Umcodierung nennt die Werte, die sie erwartet, und macht alles andere zu einem fehlenden Wert. So fällt eine Überraschung wie U beim Geschlecht auf, statt stillschweigend zu «Male» zu werden.

RPython



# Datumsangaben kommen als Excel-Seriennummern ("42010"), als ISO-Datum ("2015-04-21")
# oder als Schweizer Text mit dem Tag zuerst ("13.01.15", "13.1.2015"). Zuerst die
# Seriennummern, dann die ISO-Daten, den Rest lesen wir mit dem Tag zuerst.
parse_messy_date <- function(x, day_first = TRUE) {
  serial <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{5}$")
  iso    <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")
  rest   <- !is.na(x) & !serial & !iso
  out <- as.Date(rep(NA, length(x)))
  out[serial] <- janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(as.numeric(x[serial]))
  out[iso]    <- ymd(x[iso])
  out[rest]   <- if (day_first) dmy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE) else mdy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE)
  out
}

  rename(procedure_text = procedure) |>   # den Rohtext behalten, bis wir ihn aufgeteilt haben

    surgery_date = parse_messy_date(dos),

    sex          = case_when(str_detect(sex, regex("^f", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Female",

import numpy as np

def number(text):
    # Die erste Zahl in jeder Zelle: «67 yo» -> 67, «BMI 31.2» -> 31.2
    return pd.to_numeric(text.str.extract(r"(\d+\.?\d*)")[0])

asa_roman = {"I": "1", "II": "2", "III": "3", "IV": "4"}
procedure_text = step3["procedure"]   # den Rohtext behalten, bis wir ihn aufgeteilt haben

def parse_messy_date(col, dayfirst=True):
    """Every cell arrives as text: ISO dates ("2015-04-21", and real Excel dates as
    "2015-01-06 00:00:00") or Swiss day-first dates ("13.01.15", "13.1.2015").
    dayfirst=True would also flip ISO dates, so they're read on their own."""
    iso = col.str.match(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", na=False)
    swiss = col.notna() & ~iso
    dates = pd.concat([pd.to_datetime(col[iso], format="ISO8601"),
                       pd.to_datetime(col[swiss], format="mixed", dayfirst=dayfirst)])
    return dates.reindex(col.index)   # zurück in der Zeilenreihenfolge; leere Zellen bleiben fehlend (NaT)

tidy = pd.DataFrame({
    "case_id":      step3["study_id"].str.strip(),
    "site":         step3["site"],
    "surgery_date": parse_messy_date(step3["dos"]),
    "age":          number(step3["age"]),
    "sex":          step3["sex"].str[0].str.lower().map({"f": "Female", "m": "Male"}),
    "bmi":          number(step3["bmi"]),
    "asa":          pd.to_numeric(step3["asa"].str.replace("ASA ", "").replace(asa_roman)),
    "diabetes":     step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bDM\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "hypertension": step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bHTN\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "sleep_apnea":  step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bOSA\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "procedure":    np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"TKA|knee", case=False),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"THA|hip", case=False)],
                              ["TKA", "THA"], default=None),          # alles andere -> fehlend
    "side":         np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:L|Left)\b"),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:R|Right)\b")],
                              ["L", "R"], default=None),
    "los_days":     number(step3["los"]),
    "revised":      step3["study_id"].str.strip().isin(revised_ids).astype(int),
    "prom_preop_date": parse_messy_date(step3["prom_preop_date"]),
    "prom_preop":      number(step3["prom_preop"]),
    "prom_1yr_date":   parse_messy_date(step3["prom_1yr_date"]),
    "prom_1yr":        number(step3["prom_1yr"]),
}).sort_values(["site", "case_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)

Tipp🔀 R oder Python: Datumsangaben



R braucht für die Excel-Seriennummern einen eigenen Schritt (janitor::excel_numeric_to_date()). pandas hat diese Zellen schon in Datum-Uhrzeit-Text (2015-01-06 00:00:00) umgewandelt, den seine Funktion parse_messy_date() zusammen mit den übrigen ISO-Daten liest. Beide lesen "13.01.15" mit dem Tag zuerst: das ist der Schweizer Stil, den die Tabellen am HFR verwenden. Beide lesen ISO-Daten für sich, weil dayfirst=True in pandas auch diese vertauschen würde (2015-11-02 würde zum 11. Februar).

Einen Umfrage-Export umformen
data/messy_survey_export.csv ist das, was Umfrageplattformen liefern: eine Zeile pro Patientin oder Patient, eine Spalte pro Frage und Kontrolle (KOOS_Q3_6wk) und eine zweite Kopfzeile mit den Fragetexten. Für die Auswertung brauchen wir eine Zeile pro Person, Kontrolle und Item.

survey_path <- "data/messy_survey_export.csv"

header <- read_lines(survey_path, n_max = 1) |> str_split_1(",")
wide <- read_csv(survey_path, skip = 2, col_names = header,          # beide Kopfzeilen überspringen
                 col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

items <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    -c(ResponseId, case_id, instrument),
    names_to = c("inst", "item", "visit"),
    names_pattern = "(KOOS|HOOS)_Q(\\d)_(.*)",       # «KOOS_Q3_6wk» -> KOOS, 3, 6wk
    values_to = "response"
  ) |>
  filter(substr(instrument, 1, 4) == inst) |>         # bei jeder Person nur ihr eigenes Instrument behalten
  mutate(item = as.integer(item), response = as.integer(response),
         visit_order = match(visit, c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"))) |>
  arrange(case_id, visit_order, item) |>
  select(case_id, instrument, visit, item, response)

Wie eine Prüfung aussieht, die anschlägt
Angenommen, wir hätten die Datumsangaben der Operationen versehentlich mit dem Monat zuerst gelesen (amerikanischer Stil, wie in vielen Beispielen im Internet). Nichts stürzt ab. Zwei Prüfungen finden den Fehler: das Zählen der fehlenden Werte (Prüfung 2, auf die Datumsangaben angewendet) und eine neue Logikprüfung, ob jeder präoperative PROM-Score innerhalb eines Monats vor der Operation liegt.

RPython



wrong <- parse_messy_date(step3$dos, day_first = FALSE)   # der Fehler
preop <- parse_messy_date(step3$prom_preop_date)

outside_window <- function(surgery) {
  days_before <- as.numeric(surgery - preop)
  sum(days_before < 0 | days_before > 31, na.rm = TRUE)
}
c(missing_correct     = sum(is.na(tidy$surgery_date)),
  missing_month_first = sum(is.na(wrong)),
  window_correct      = outside_window(parse_messy_date(step3$dos)),
  window_month_first  = outside_window(wrong))

    missing_correct missing_month_first      window_correct  window_month_first 
                  0                  30                   0                  12 





wrong = parse_messy_date(step3["dos"], dayfirst=False)   # der Fehler
preop = parse_messy_date(step3["prom_preop_date"])

def outside_window(surgery):
    days_before = (surgery - preop).dt.days
    return int(((days_before < 0) | (days_before > 31)).sum())

print(pd.Series({
    "missing_correct": tidy["surgery_date"].isna().sum(),
    "missing_month_first": wrong.isna().sum(),
    "window_correct": outside_window(parse_messy_date(step3["dos"])),
    "window_month_first": outside_window(wrong),
}))

Beim richtigen Einlesen fehlt nichts, und jeder präoperative PROM-Score liegt in seinem Zeitfenster. Die Versionen mit dem Monat zuerst gehen auf verschiedene Arten schief:

R kann Datumsangaben wie "13.01.15" nicht mit dem Monat zuerst lesen (einen 13. Monat gibt es nicht), darum fehlen 30 Datumsangaben der Operationen. Andere, etwa "04.03.24", werden «erfolgreich» als 3. April statt als 4. März eingelesen, und die Prüfung des Zeitfensters meldet 12 davon.
pandas liefert hier nie ein fehlendes Datum: Wenn der Monat zuerst unmöglich ist, wechselt es stillschweigend zum Tag zuerst. So kommt "13.01.15" durch Zufall richtig heraus, während "04.03.24" zum 3. April wird. Nur die Prüfung des Zeitfensters bemerkt es: Sie meldet 12 Datumsangaben.







Warnung⚠️ Achtung: eine einzige Prüfung genügt nie



Lesen Sie eine Spalte mit gemischten Formaten nie mit einer einzigen Einstellung ein: Lesen Sie jedes Format für sich, wie es parse_messy_date() tut. Beachten Sie auch, dass das Zählen der fehlenden Werte diesen Fehler in R fand, in Python aber nicht, während ihn die Logikprüfung in beiden fand. Führen Sie jedes Mal alle Prüfungen durch; sie finden verschiedene Fehler.




Zum Schluss: mit dem Lösungsschlüssel vergleichen
Weil dies ein Datensatz zum Üben ist, gibt es eine bekannte richtige Antwort: data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv. Unser Resultat stimmt genau damit überein.
